## Proof

**Setup.** The "first uncountable ordinal" is $\omega_1$. The set of ordinals below $\omega_1$ is the set of all countable ordinals, which has cardinality $\aleph_1$. We assume a uniform probability measure $\mu$ on $\omega_1$ (i.e., a measure that is translation-invariant in the ordinal sense and assigns measure 0 to singletons, hence to every countable set). Two independent draws $n_1, n_2 \sim \mu$ are made. Player two wins iff $n_2 > n_1$.

**Key fact.** Every ordinal $\alpha < \omega_1$ is countable. Therefore, for any fixed $\alpha < \omega_1$, the initial segment
$$\{\beta \in \omega_1 : \beta \leq \alpha\} = \alpha + 1$$
is a countable set (it is a countable successor ordinal). Since $\mu$ is uniform on an uncountable set, every countable subset has $\mu$-measure $0$.

**Computing the probability.** Conditioning on $n_1 = \alpha$:
$$P(n_2 > n_1 \mid n_1 = \alpha) = P(n_2 > \alpha) = 1 - P(n_2 \leq \alpha) = 1 - \mu(\{\beta : \beta \leq \alpha\}) = 1 - 0 = 1.$$

This holds for **every** countable ordinal $\alpha < \omega_1$. By the law of total probability (Tonelli's theorem, since the integrand is non-negative):
$$P(n_2 > n_1) = \int_{\omega_1} P(n_2 > \alpha)\, d\mu(\alpha) = \int_{\omega_1} 1\, d\mu(\alpha) = 1.$$

**The paradox and its resolution.** By the identical argument with roles swapped, $P(n_1 > n_2) = 1$ as well. Since $P(n_1 = n_2) = 0$ (singletons have measure 0), we would get
$$P(n_2 > n_1) + P(n_1 > n_2) + P(n_1 = n_2) = 1 + 1 + 0 = 2 \neq 1,$$
a contradiction. This reveals that **no uniform probability measure exists on $\omega_1$** — the assumption in the problem is inconsistent. The obstruction is fundamental: $\omega_1$ is not measurable in the sense required (there is no $\sigma$-additive, translation-invariant probability measure on $\omega_1$ that vanishes on singletons; this follows because $\omega_1$ has uncountable cofinality, so any such measure would have to assign measure 0 to every initial segment yet measure 1 to the whole, which is impossible for a $\sigma$-additive measure on a set of size $\aleph_1$).

**Answer.** Under the stated (inconsistent) assumption of a uniform density, the conditional argument forces:

$$\boxed{P(\text{player two wins}) = P(n_2 > n_1) = 1.}$$

For any countable ordinal that player one hits, the set of ordinals at or below it is countable and thus has measure zero under the uniform density, so player two almost surely hits a larger ordinal. The fact that the symmetric argument also yields probability 1 demonstrates that the premise — a uniform probability measure on $\omega_1$ — cannot actually be realized.

### PROOF COMPLETE
